newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam Tamexco trial prompts blast against graft.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam Tamexco trial prompts blast against graft.

text.p: Vietnam's biggest corruption trial entered its second day on Friday accompanied by a media onslaught against graft and calls for the judiciary to halt "declining confidence" in the communist government.
Official newspapers splashed coverage of the first day's proceedings across front pages. Photographs showed grim-faced defendants with bowed heads. Several are on trial for their lives.

"The penal code of Vietnam specifies that the embezzlement of State assets and bribery are subject to the highest punishment -- the death sentence," said the Saigon Times Daily, leaving little room for doubt over the outcome.

The trial, which has sent shockwaves through the political establishment, centres on allegations that the 20 defendants siphoned off millions of dollars from Tamexco -- a Ho Chi Minh City trading firm with links to the ruling Communist Party.
The company director and a circle of his colleagues, relatives and friends stand accused along with state officials and senior bankers.
Adding further fuel to the scandal are widely reported links between those who have been implicated and some of the most powerful people in the country.

But in an apparent sign of Hanoi's determination to showcase its anti-graft resolve, Friday's official Vietnam News daily led with a call by National Assembly Chairman Nong Duc Manh for judicial courage in punishing those involved in such cases.

Manh, who ranks fourth in the elite Politburo, said the legal system should expose violations of judicial procedures and civil rights while working to root out and punish people who indulge in corruption.
"Only by doing this can the control body help restore people's declining confidence in the state and government," he was quoted as saying.

Manh added that illegal detention, the use of torture to force confessions and what he described as biased verdicts in corruption and smuggling cases had triggered indignation and undermined public confidence.
He called for a strict evaluation of personnel involved in Vietnam's judicial and police systems "so that 'degraded' elements could be 'weeded out'".

The Tamexco trial, which is expected to run for at least a week, has been closed to foreign journalists. But the focus of attention is likely to be on how far Hanoi is prepared to allow the implications of the case to go.
Domestic newspapers have called for several other officials to be brought into the net for influence peddling.

According to Friday's Lao Dong (Labour) newspaper, 63 people connected to the case have been asked to be present in court, including the deputy governor at the central State Bank of Vietnam -- Chu Van Nguyen.
The paper reported that the lead defendant, Pham Huy Phuoc, had asked for the state prosecutor to be replaced on grounds that he was too aggressive. The request was turned down.
